nodes.name: Relation edge sets on a common user set
nodes.statement: We consider different sets of edges $\mathcal{E}=\{E_1, \ldots, E_Q\}$ on a common set of users $V$.

nodes.name: Relation graph G_i
nodes.statement: Each $E_i$ captures a symmetric relation between users, such as friendship or group co-membership. $(V, E_i)$ thus defines an undirected graph $G_i$ on $V$.

nodes.name: Union (simple) graph
nodes.statement: The {\em union (simple) graph} $G'=(V,E')$ of $G_1,\ldots,G_Q$ is defined as the graph on $V$, whose edges are given by the set $E'=\cup_{i=1}^Q E_i$. \hfill $\blacksquare$
differentia: whose edges are given by the set $E'=\cup_{i=1}^Q E_i$
nodes.label: def:uniongraph

nodes.name: Union multigraph
nodes.statement: The {\em union multigraph} $G=(V,E)$ of $G_1,\ldots,G_Q$ is defined as the multigraph on $V$, whose edges are given by the multiset $E=\biguplus_{i=1}^Q E_i$. \hfill $\blacksquare$
differentia: whose edges are given by the multiset $E=\biguplus_{i=1}^Q E_i$
nodes.statement_short: The multigraph on $V$ whose edge multiset is the disjoint (multiset) union of all relation edge sets.
nodes.label: def:multigraph

nodes.name: Multigraph vs union graph edges
nodes.statement: Note that the union multigraph $G$ can contain multiple edges between a pair of nodes, while the union graph $G'$ contains only one (or no) edge.

nodes.name: Reduction of multigraph to union graph
nodes.statement: Every multigraph $G$ can be reduced to the union graph $G'$ by merging together multiple edges between two nodes into one.

nodes.name: Naive multiple graph sampling
nodes.statement: A naive way is to run many random walks, one per each individual graph~$G_i$, and to combine the collected samples.
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: run a separate random walk on each relation graph $G_i$ and pool the samples.

nodes.name: Bias of naive multiple graph sampling
nodes.statement: However, if a particular~$G_i$ is disconnected (as are all five graphs in Fig.~\ref{fig:bernoulli-example}(a-e)), a walk on $G_i$ is restricted to the connected component around its starting point and thus never converges to the desired target distribution. This results in an asymptotically biased sample, dependent on the initial seeds.
conclusions: a walk on $G_i$ is restricted to the connected component around its starting point and thus never converges to the desired target distribution
This results in an asymptotically biased sample, dependent on the initial seeds.
nodes.statement_short: A walk on a disconnected $G_i$ stays in its seed's component, so naive pooling gives an asymptotically seed-dependent biased sample.

nodes.name: Union simple graph sampling
nodes.statement: A much better approach is to perform a random walk on the union graph~$G'$.
nodes.statement_short: Random walk on the union simple graph $G'$ of all relations.

nodes.name: Cost of union graph walk
nodes.statement: A potential practical difficulty with a random walk on the union graph~$G'$ is that, at each step, computing the neighborhood union can be quite expensive: it requires the enumeration of all edges adjacent to the current vertex~$v$, in each relation graph~$G_i$. This may be very costly, depending on $v$'s neighborhood size (which can be large in heavily clustered relations, such as group co-membership), query costs, and the number of relations~$Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Each step of a union-graph walk must enumerate the neighbours of $v$ in every relation graph, which can be costly.

nodes.name: Relation degree and total multigraph degree
nodes.statement: Denote by $d_i(v)$ the degree of node $v$ in graph~$G_i$, and by $d(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{Q} d_i(v)$ its total degree in the union multigraph.

nodes.name: Multigraph Sampling Algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{Multigraph Sampling Algorithm} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \REQUIRE {$v_0\in V$, simple graphs $G_i, i=1\ldots Q$} \STATE {Initialize $v \leftarrow v_0$.} \WHILE{\textsc{not Converged}} \STATE {Select graph $G_i$ with probability $\frac{d_i(v)}{d(v)}$} \STATE {Select uniformly at random a neighbor $v'$ of $v$ in $G_i$} \STATE {$v \leftarrow v'$} \ENDWHILE \RETURN{all sampled nodes $v$ and their degrees $d(v)$.} \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Two-stage random walk on the union multigraph: pick relation $G_i$ with probability $d_i(v)/d(v)$, then a uniform neighbour of $v$ in $G_i$.
output: all sampled nodes $v$ and their degrees $d(v)$.
also_stated_at: First, we select a graph~$G_i$ with probability $\frac{d_i(v)}{d(v)}$. Second, we pick uniformly at random an edge of $v$ within the selected~$G_i$ ({\em i.e., } with prob. $\frac{1}{d_i(v)}$), and we follow this edge to $v$'s neighbor.

nodes.name: Initialize current node
nodes.statement: {Initialize $v \leftarrow v_0$.}

nodes.name: Walk until convergence
nodes.statement: \WHILE{\textsc{not Converged}} \STATE {Select graph $G_i$ with probability $\frac{d_i(v)}{d(v)}$} \STATE {Select uniformly at random a neighbor $v'$ of $v$ in $G_i$} \STATE {$v \leftarrow v'$}
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the two-stage neighbour selection until convergence.

nodes.name: Select relation graph
nodes.statement: {Select graph $G_i$ with probability $\frac{d_i(v)}{d(v)}$}
nodes.statement_short: Choose relation $G_i$ with probability proportional to $d_i(v)$.

nodes.name: Select neighbour in chosen graph
nodes.statement: {Select uniformly at random a neighbor $v'$ of $v$ in $G_i$}

nodes.name: Move to neighbour
nodes.statement: {$v \leftarrow v'$}

nodes.name: Return samples
nodes.statement: \RETURN{all sampled nodes $v$ and their degrees $d(v)$.}

nodes.name: Two-stage selection equals uniform multigraph edge selection
nodes.statement: This procedure is equivalent to selecting an edge of $v$ uniformly at random in the union multigraph, because $\frac{d_i(v)}{d(v)} \cdot \frac{1}{d_i(v)} = \frac{1}{d(v)}$.
conclusions: This procedure is equivalent to selecting an edge of $v$ uniformly at random in the union multigraph
nodes.statement_short: Choosing relation $i$ w.p. $d_i(v)/d(v)$ then a uniform edge in it picks each multigraph edge of $v$ w.p. $1/d(v)$.

nodes.name: Bandwidth savings of Algorithm 1
nodes.statement: Note that in Step~3, Algorithm~\ref{alg:mixture} requires only the values of degrees~$d_i(v)$ of all relation graphs. Only in Step~4 of Algorithm~\ref{alg:mixture} does one enumerate all neighboring edges in the selected~$G_i$. Because the degree information~$d_i(v)$ is usually much cheaper to obtain ({\em e.g., } via simple low-bandwidth API calls) than enumerating all~$d_i(v)$ edges, Algorithm~\ref{alg:mixture} has the potential to save much bandwidth compared to the union simple graph sampling (which enumerates all neighboring edges in all relations). This benefit is amplified when higher numbers of relations ($Q$) are used.
nodes.statement_short: Algorithm 1 needs only per-relation degrees plus one relation's neighbour list per step, saving bandwidth versus union-graph sampling.

nodes.name: Equilibrium distribution of multigraph sampling
nodes.statement: If $G$ is connected and contains at least one triangle, then Algorithm~\ref{alg:mixture} leads to equilibrium distribution $\pi(v)=\frac{d(v)}{\sum_{u\in V} d(u)}$.
assumptions: $G$ is connected and contains at least one triangle
conclusions: Algorithm~\ref{alg:mixture} leads to equilibrium distribution $\pi(v)=\frac{d(v)}{\sum_{u\in V} d(u)}$
also_stated_at: We prove that this algorithm achieves convergence to the proper equilibrium distribution when the union multigraph is connected.
nodes.statement_short: Under connectivity and aperiodicity (a triangle), the multigraph walk has stationary distribution proportional to total degree $d(v)$.
nodes.label: lemma:equilibrium

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: Let $d(v,u)=d(u,v)$ be the number of edges between nodes $v$ and $u$ in the union multigraph $G$. The sampling process of Algorithm~\ref{alg:mixture} is a Markov chain on $V$ with transition probabilities $P_{vu}=\frac{d(v,u)}{d(v)}, u,v \in V$. So long as $G$ is finite and connected, this random walk is irreducible and positive recurrent. The presence of a triangle within $G$ further guarantees aperiodicity. A Markov chain of this type is equivalent to a random walk on an undirected weighted graph with edge weights $w(v,u)=d(v,u)$. A random walk on weighted graph is known to have the unique equilibrium distribution $\pi(v)=\frac{w(v)}{\sum_{u\in V} w(u)}$, where $w(v)=\sum_{u} w(v,u)$ ({\em e.g., } see \cite[Example 4.32]{RossBook}), and the proof follows immediately by substitution.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the walk as a reversible Markov chain on a weighted graph with weights $d(v,u)$ and substitute into the known weighted-walk stationary law.

nodes.name: Define multiplicities $d(v,u)$ and write the walk as a Marko
nodes.statement: Let $d(v,u)=d(u,v)$ be the number of edges between nodes $v$ and $u$ in the union multigraph $G$. The sampling process of Algorithm~\ref{alg:mixture} is a Markov chain on $V$ with transition probabilities $P_{vu}=\frac{d(v,u)}{d(v)}, u,v \in V$.
nodes.statement_short: Define multiplicities $d(v,u)$ and write the walk as a Markov chain with $P_{vu}=d(v,u)/d(v)$.

nodes.name: Connectivity gives irreducibility and positive recurrence
nodes.statement: So long as $G$ is finite and connected, this random walk is irreducible and positive recurrent. The presence of a triangle within $G$ further guarantees aperiodicity.
nodes.statement_short: Connectivity gives irreducibility and positive recurrence; a triangle gives aperiodicity.

nodes.statement: A Markov chain of this type is equivalent to a random walk on an undirected weighted graph with edge weights $w(v,u)=d(v,u)$.
nodes.statement_short: Recast as a random walk on a weighted graph with weights $d(v,u)$.

nodes.statement: A random walk on weighted graph is known to have the unique equilibrium distribution $\pi(v)=\frac{w(v)}{\sum_{u\in V} w(u)}$, where $w(v)=\sum_{u} w(v,u)$ ({\em e.g., } see \cite[Example 4.32]{RossBook}), and the proof follows immediately by substitution.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the known weighted-walk stationary distribution and substitute.

nodes.name: RWRW more efficient than Metropolis-Hastings random walk
nodes.statement: In \cite{Gjoka2011_Facebook_JSAC}, we showed that a simple random walk with correction for unequal sample weights, also called Re-Weighted Random Walk (RWRW), is more efficient than competitors such as Metropolis-Hastings Random Walks.
conclusions: a simple random walk with correction for unequal sample weights, also called Re-Weighted Random Walk (RWRW), is more efficient than competitors such as Metropolis-Hastings Random Walks

nodes.name: Degree bias of multigraph random walk
nodes.statement: Much like a classic random walk on a simple graph, a random walk on multigraph~$G$ is inherently biased towards high-degree nodes. Indeed, per Proposition~\ref{lemma:equilibrium}, the probability of sampling a node~$v$ is proportional to its degree~$d(v)$ in~$G$.

nodes.name: Hansen-Hurwitz estimator
nodes.statement: Let~$x(v)$ be an arbitrary function defined on graph nodes~$V$, with mean $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{|V|}\sum_{v \in V} x(v).$ Then \begin{equation} \hat{\bar{x}}\ =\ \frac{\sum_{v \in S} x(v)/d(v)}{\sum_{v \in S} 1/d(v)} \end{equation} is an unbiased and consistent estimator of~$\bar{x}$.
assumptions: Let~$x(v)$ be an arbitrary function defined on graph nodes~$V$, with mean $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{|V|}\sum_{v \in V} x(v).$
conclusions: is an unbiased and consistent estimator of~$\bar{x}$
nodes.statement_short: Weighting each sampled node by $1/d(v)$ gives a ratio estimator of the population mean of $x$ that corrects degree bias.

nodes.name: Re-weighted mean estimator
nodes.statement: \hat{\bar{x}}\ =\ \frac{\sum_{v \in S} x(v)/d(v)}{\sum_{v \in S} 1/d(v)}

nodes.name: Re-Weighted Random Walk (RWRW)
nodes.statement: By default, we use this reweighting procedure throughput the paper (referring to the combination of random walks with post-hoc reweighting as the RWRW method).

nodes.name: Geweke diagnostic
nodes.statement: Second, we use the Geweke \cite{geweke} diagnostic within each random walk, which verifies that mean values for scalar parameters at the beginning of the walk (here the first 10\% of samples) does not differ significantly from the corresponding mean at the end of the walk (here the last 50\%).
nodes.statement_short: Within-walk convergence check comparing the mean over the first 10% of samples with the mean over the last 50%.

nodes.name: Gelman-Rubin diagnostic
nodes.statement: Third, we use the Gelman-Rubin \cite{gelman-rubin} diagnostic to verify convergence across walks, by ensuring that the parameter variance between walks matches the variance within walks.
nodes.statement_short: Across-walk convergence check that the between-walk variance matches the within-walk variance.

nodes.name: Largest connected component fraction f_LCC
nodes.statement: In order to characterize the connectivity of $G$, we define $f_{LCC}$ as the fraction of nodes that belong to the largest connected component in~$G$.

nodes.name: Multigraph of six ER graphs is connected
nodes.statement: With a relatively small number of simple graphs, say for $Q=6$, we get $f_{LCC}\simeq1$, which means that the multigraph is fully connected with high probability.

nodes.name: Union of random graphs crosses the connectivity threshold
nodes.statement: Given $Q$ independent random graphs with $N$ nodes each and with expected densities $p_1,\ldots,p_Q$, the probability that an edge $\{u,v\}$ belongs to their union graph $G'$ is $p^*=1-\prod_{i=1}^Q(1-p_i)$. For $p_i$ approximately equal, this approaches~1 exponentially fast in $Q$. Asymptotically, the union graph will be almost surely connected where $(N-1) p^*> \ln N$ \cite[pp413--417]{West96}, in which case the union multigraph is also trivially connected. Thus, intuitively, a relatively small number of sparse graphs are needed for the union to exceed its connectivity threshold.
nodes.statement_short: The union of $Q$ random graphs has edge probability $1-\prod(1-p_i)$, so it crosses the $\ln N/N$ connectivity threshold for small $Q$.

nodes.name: Second eigenvalue lambda_2
nodes.statement: In order to characterize the mixing time, we plot the second eigenvalue $\lambda_2$ of the transition matrix of the random walk (on the LCC).

nodes.name: lambda_2 relates to mixing time
nodes.statement: $\lambda_2$ is well-known to relate to the mixing time of the associated Markov chain \cite{Boyd2004_mixing}: the smaller $\lambda_2$, the faster the convergence.
conclusions: the smaller $\lambda_2$, the faster the convergence

nodes.name: lambda_2 decreases with Q
nodes.statement: In Fig.~\ref{fig:ER_graphs}(top), we observe that $\lambda_2$ significantly drops with growing~$Q$.

nodes.name: Adding edges need not decrease lambda_2
nodes.statement: (However, note that adding a new edge to an existing graph does not always guarantee the decrease of $\lambda_2$. It is possible to design examples where $\lambda_2$ increases, although they are rare.)

nodes.name: Estimation error decreases with Q
nodes.statement: This error decreases not only with the walk length, but also with the number $Q$ of combined graphs.
conclusions: This error decreases not only with the walk length, but also with the number $Q$ of combined graphs.

nodes.name: Multigraph sampling robust to cliques
nodes.statement: Interestingly, the multigraph technique is efficient also under the presence of cliques.
conclusions: the multigraph technique is efficient also under the presence of cliques

nodes.name: Crawl types
nodes.statement: In the rest of the section, we refer to random walks on different simple graphs or multigraphs as {\em crawl types}.

nodes.name: Uniform rejection sampling of userIDs (UNI)
nodes.statement: Specifically, each user was sampled by repeatedly drawing uniform integers between $0$ and $35$ million ({\em i.e., } the maximum observed ID plus a $\sim$4 million ``safety'' range) and querying the userID space. Integers not corresponding to a valid userID were discarded, with the process being repeated until a match was obtained.
nodes.statement_short: Rejection sampling: draw uniform integers in $[0, 35M]$, query the userID, discard invalid IDs, repeat until a valid user is found.

nodes.name: Draw a uniform integer ID
nodes.statement: repeatedly drawing uniform integers between $0$ and $35$ million ({\em i.e., } the maximum observed ID plus a $\sim$4 million ``safety'' range)

nodes.name: Query the userID
nodes.statement: querying the userID space

nodes.name: Discard invalid IDs and repeat
nodes.statement: Integers not corresponding to a valid userID were discarded, with the process being repeated until a match was obtained

nodes.name: Rejection-sampled IDs are uniform
nodes.statement: IDs obtained in this way are uniformly sampled from the space of user accounts, irrespective of how IDs are actually allocated within the address space \cite{Gjoka2011_multigraph_JSAC}.
conclusions: IDs obtained in this way are uniformly sampled from the space of user accounts, irrespective of how IDs are actually allocated within the address space

nodes.name: UNI sample
nodes.statement: We employ this procedure to obtain a sample of 500K users, referred to here as ``UNI.''

nodes.name: Capture-recapture estimate of Last.fm population
nodes.statement: According to this method, the population size is estimated to be : $$ P_{{\tt Last.fm}\xspace} = \frac{N_{UNI1}\times N_{UNI2}}{R} = 28.5M,$$ where $N_{UNI1} = N_{UNI2} = 500K$ and $R$ is the number of valid common userIDs sampled during the first and second UNI samples.
assumptions: $N_{UNI1} = N_{UNI2} = 500K$ and $R$ is the number of valid common userIDs sampled during the first and second UNI samples
nodes.statement_short: Capture-recapture (Lincoln-Petersen) estimate $N_1N_2/R$ from two UNI samples gives about 28.5M users.

nodes.name: Small user growth during crawls
nodes.statement: Therefore, with a population increase of $0.09\%/$day, the user growth during our crawls (2-7 days) is calculated to range between $0.18\%-0.63\%$ per crawl type, which is quite small.
conclusions: the user growth during our crawls (2-7 days) is calculated to range between $0.18\%-0.63\%$ per crawl type

nodes.name: Static network during crawling
nodes.statement: Therefore, in the rest of the paper, we assume that any changes in the {\tt Last.fm}\xspace network during the crawling period can be ignored.

nodes.name: Two-stage multigraph sampling implementation for Last.fm
nodes.statement: In the first stage, we discover the graphs of user $u$, and $u$'s degrees in them. In our study, we use the API calls {\tt user.getfriends}, {\tt user.getneighbors}, {\tt user.getpastevents}, and {\tt user.getevents} to collect the list of friends, neighbors, past events, and future events respectively. Due to a lack of an API call that lists the groups of a user, we use data scraping to collect the list of groups and corresponding size for each group. We treat each individual group and event as a different graph in the multigraph. We also consider the set of friends and neighbors to comprise the friends and neighbors graph respectively in the multigraph. At the end of the first stage, we select one of the graphs $G_i$ in accordance with Algorithm~\ref{alg:mixture} in Section~\ref{sec:mg_samplingmethodology}. We should note that at the end of the first stage, we have not enumerated any user from any of the groups and events graphs. Each of these graphs is quite large (up to tens of thousands of users) and depending on the user, there are many groups or events per user (up to thousands). On the other hand, we have enumerated users of friends and neighbors since knowledge of neighborhood size is equivalent to enumeration \footnote{There might be workarounds to enumerating friends but they are not necessarily more efficient. For example, we could extract the number of friends by data scraping. In general, in another setting we could do away with any kind of enumeration in the first stage.} for these graphs. Overall, our two stage approach saves us bandwidth and time by avoiding the enumeration of users for graphs that we are not going to sample from at each iteration. In the second stage, we pick uniformly at random one of the nodes from the graph $G_i$, selected at the end of the first stage. If the graph $G_i$ is a graph of a group or an event, we need to carefully implement this action to be efficient. More specifically, we do not need to enumerate all group members or event attendants from a group or event graph. Instead, we can take advantage of the pages functionality that OSNs often provide and only fetch the page that corresponds to the user selected uniformly at random. In our study, to fetch group members we use the API call {\tt group.getmembers}, which returns 50 users per page. To fetch event attendants we use data scraping\footnote{We prefer data scraping to the API call {\tt event.getattendees} because the API call i) is not paged ii) does not return users that marked ``maybe`` for the event iii) is very slow for large events.}, which also returns 50 users per HTML page.
nodes.statement_short: Stage 1 queries per-relation degrees of $u$ (treating each group/event as a graph) and picks a relation per Algorithm 1; stage 2 fetches only the API page holding a uniformly chosen member.

nodes.name: Convergence diagnostics cannot detect biased equilibrium
nodes.statement: This underscores an important point regarding convergence diagnostics: while useful for determining whether a random walk sample approximates its equilibrium distribution, they cannot reliably identify cases in which the equilibrium itself is biased ({\em e.g., } due to non-connectivity).

nodes.name: Selection of relations for multigraph sampling
nodes.statement: Open questions include the selection of a few -out of many candidate- relations to use when sampling, so as to optimize the multigraph sampler performance.

nodes.name: Negatively correlated relations are most effective
nodes.statement: Intuitively, we expect that negatively correlated relations will prove most effective.
conclusions: negatively correlated relations will prove most effective
